background_work.note: M5 row timers and M8 backfills/digests worked, including closed-client restart verification. M6 logged backend defects for unsupported string operations and dropped HTTP headers; push presence additionally required a heartbeat with delayed disconnect detection.

snapback2.verdict: Strong integrated primitives were undermined by published-surface constraints and recovery gaps that materially compromised this brief.
snapback2.would_use_again_for: I would use it again for bounded reactive applications benefiting from integrated offline queues and timers, after validating their asset-lifecycle requirements against the published limits.

writes_and_transactions.note: M2/M3 transactions directly supported set-state deduplication, counters, DM uniqueness and recipient capture. M8 updated Insights with source writes and persisted digest completion atomically. No transactional backend defect was demonstrated.

offline_sync.note: M6/M8 web convergence passed, but the lane authored its durable outbox, account-scoped caches, media persistence and purge policies. The published surface supplied no complete offline database or durable queue; native behavior remained unverified.

convex.would_use_again_for: I would use it again for reactive messaging and collaboration applications with a separately planned durable offline layer.

overall.note: M1–M8 delivered green web results, eventual native offline proofs and verified corpus state. SQL, managed Auth and Storage were effective; the essay documents substantial custom synchronization, authorization routing and worker/process responsibilities.

The diary records manually integrated HTTP refresh, subscriptions for presence, token lifecycle, cache reconciliation and reconnect behavior; polling bugs are excluded as backend defects.

diagnostics_dev_loop.note: The run log records actionable rate-limit documentation, correct expired-principal refusal and useful SQL EXPLAIN inspection. The final report establishes no Supabase defect; native observability and unhandled pool errors were application corrections.

Documented Auth pacing constrained replay, while unpaced requests and recovery mistakes were agent-error. Staged/resumed replay qualification remains unresolved.

supabase.verdict: Supabase was an excellent relational foundation for Clique, while this deployment left much of the live, offline and worker integration to application code.
supabase.would_use_again_for: I would use it again for relational social products where SQL reporting and explicit control justify owning synchronization and worker services.

cross_backend_notes: These judgments exclude agent-error, environment and ambiguous incident costs; elapsed time and correction counts are not treated as backend rankings.

Convex required the least assembly for connected transactions, live queries and scheduling, while Supabase's SQL model was especially direct for relationships and reporting; Supabase Realtime was not exercised.

Snapback supplied the strongest integrated offline machinery, but query ceilings, missing server one-use assets and effect-header defects forced workarounds; its staging penalty concerns missing recovery tooling rather than the ambiguous accumulation cause.
Supabase's eventual native proofs validate its custom persistence implementation; missing equivalent proofs in Snapback and Convex are evidence gaps rather than demonstrated backend failures.
All three reached verified full-corpus state with differing replay qualifications, none establishes complete O5 or comparable latency, and M7 was unrun everywhere.

supabase.verdict: Hosted Postgres and Auth were a fast M1; the messenger brief after that is an application you write, and this lane's two-browser live bar never recovered.
supabase.would_use_again_for: A refresh-based CRUD social app on Postgres where GoTrue is the win, not a 2-second typing/live-DM messenger or a durable offline queue.

cross_backend_notes: Convex was the only Grok lane to green M1–M8 choreography and finish the 167157-action scale replay; Snapback and Supabase both passed scripted suites through M8 but lost the two-browser live bar at M3 (Snapback) or M2 (Supabase).

Snapback uniquely expressed membership, typing TTL, row expiry, and offline retain as schema, then the 4MiB certified merge (~360 follows), 40-object asset ceiling, and Expo snapback2/react export fought the brief's envelope and web client.

Supabase uniquely bought password auth and SQL constraints in hour one, then reimplemented live (poll), offline (localStorage), digest (Node setInterval), and media refusal (byte proxy) because hosted-without-CLI Realtime, Edge, and Storage policy were not operable as product features.
All three paid RN-web/Playwright observability (agent-error); only Snapback's Metro export and 256-subscription cap and Convex's non-ticking queries were charged as backend live-query defects.

Writes and idempotency were easy everywhere (Quarry mutation IDs, Convex mutations, SQL ON CONFLICT); what separated scores was whether live, time, offline, and media revocation were platform primitives or an application.
